title: Grief and practice
hookLine: a warm mug in two hands, and a breath that holds a hard feeling instead of fixing it
tomorrow: can you still give someone a gift after they've died?

lines: A WARM MUG IN BOTH HANDS.
cards: When someone is crying at a kitchen table, people often do the same small thing without being taught: they make tea and put the warm mug in both of the other person's hands.
Others go for a long walk, or scrub a kitchen that was already clean. None of it fixes anything. Bodies just know that a hard feeling goes better held than fought.
The Buddhist answer to what you do with grief starts in the same place, with the body: the breath, and warmth.

teach.b: Start with the breath. In the sutta on mindfulness of breathing, the practice begins very simply: breathing in long, you know it's long; breathing out short, you know it's short.

teach.h: CALMING THE BODY, BREATH BY BREATH.
teach.b: A little further on, the meditator breathes in and out calming the body. Nothing in those steps says get rid of the sadness first.

The breath goes on underneath whatever is there, steady, and you can rest on it like a hand on a railing. Some days the breath is the one thing in the room that isn't sad, and that's enough to lean on. Then add kindness.

teach.h: LIKE A MOTHER HOLDS A CHILD.
teach.b: In the discourse on loving-kindness, the picture for a boundless heart is a mother protecting her only child with her life. The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh took that picture into grief.
He taught people to hold a painful feeling the way a mother holds a crying baby: not shaking it, not shouting at it to stop, just holding it close until it settles.
Put the two together and you get a way to practice with grief. Breath underneath, kindness around. The grief doesn't have to leave for the practice to work.

teach.h: NOT A TRICK TO MAKE IT VANISH.
teach.b: Meditation here isn't a trick for making sadness vanish.
It's a way of not leaving the sad one alone, even when the sad one is you. A hospital hallway, a song in the car, a smell in a coat pocket: wherever it comes, the breath is already there.

how: Buddhist teachers often suggest returning to the breath and to loving-kindness in times of grief; some communities hold group sits or chanting after a death, where mourners practice together.

o: meeting a loss with breath and kindness instead of a fight
a ritual that ends grief once and for all in one day
a set of rules for how long a Buddhist may mourn

games.q: what holds the grief — tap the pairs.
p: a step in mindfulness of breathing
a mother protecting her only child
hold pain like a crying baby

s: meditation is a way to make sadness disappear
the steps in the sutta don't ask the sadness to leave first. the practice holds it.
the breathing sutta includes breathing in and out calming the body
a little way into the practice, the meditator breathes in and out calming the body.
Buddhist practice means emptying the mind of all feeling
the loving-kindness picture is a mother holding a child close: feeling, held with care.

games.q: you're on the bus and a wave of grief hits, out of nowhere. what does today's practice suggest?
o: push it down until you're home; practice is for quiet rooms.
feel your breath and your hands, and let the feeling be held there.
start a long meditation right away to get rid of the feeling.
games.why: the breath goes on underneath, anywhere. you don't fight the wave or fix it; you hold it, like a warm mug in both hands.

practice: If there's a warm drink near you, hold it in both hands; if not, cup one hand inside the other. Feel the warmth and the weight. Breathe in, knowing you're breathing in; breathe out, letting the shoulders soften.
If something sad comes, let it sit in your hands with the warmth.

wordCard.voice: Grief and practice: breath underneath and kindness around, holding a hard feeling the way a mother holds a crying child.

orig.note: Pali anapanasati: mindfulness of the in-breath and the out-breath.

carryVoice: Line for today: held gently, so the feeling can stay without being alone. That's seventeen days in.
